updates.alert: I'm selling Marathon Petroleum. Refining margins (the 3-2-1 crack spread) have nearly halved since their October peak as Middle East peace talks ease supply fears, so its P/E of 6.8 rests on peak profits. It is also 20 points behind the S&P 500 ETF, and selling it cuts my energy overweight from 16% to about 9.5%. I'm buying Visa, a steadier quality share (15% revenue growth, 51% net margin, 3% under its high in a falling market) that brings my financials weight close to the index's. I'm keeping CrowdStrike because its November 23 results were strong (revenue +28%, record net new annual recurring revenue, guidance raised); the drop came mainly from its $43.9 billion all-stock Zscaler deal. I'm trimming it to 6.5% for the dilution and integration risk, trimming Nucor slightly and adding to Omnicom. The main risks I'm watching are a deeper AI-chip selloff, NetApp's results on December 1 and Morgan Stanley sitting just above its exit line.
updates.market_view: The S&P 500 ETF is 8.3% below its high, and its 20-day volatility of 29.6% is more than double its 12.8% average. The damage is concentrated, though: the tech median is down 16% over a month and energy is down 11%, while 8 of 11 sectors are up and breadth has recovered to 55% from 47% at my last decision. I read this as a correction centred on AI and energy, with money rotating into defensive and quality names, not a broad breakdown. The AI-chip selloff is still going (Nvidia fell 8.7% on November 25), so I am keeping the tech underweight, cutting cyclical risk and holding a little more cash.
updates.self_review: Since November 20 the portfolio rose 1.9% against the ETF's 3.0%. Target and Omnicom are 4-5 points ahead of the ETF, but Marathon and the AI-linked names lagged. I wrongly listed CrowdStrike's results for December 1 when they came out on November 23. Of my exits, the Valero sale on falling refining margins helped by 4.5 points, while Fortinet, sold on its price rule after the drop, has since beaten the ETF by 3.9 points.

new.thesis: New: a payments network with 15% revenue growth and a 51% net margin, 2.7% under its 52-week high and 21% above its 200-day average while the index falls. It lifts my financials from 5% toward the index's 13% with a steadier share than Morgan Stanley.

considered.why_not: Sold, a broken thesis rather than an overreaction: the 3-2-1 crack spread has nearly halved since its October peak, with peace-talk expectations as the cited cause, so the P/E of 6.8 rests on peak margins that are shrinking, even if the EIA still expects margins above normal into 2027.

Too early to tell: the 32% monthly fall comes from doubts that heavy AI infrastructure spending will pay off (-8.7% on November 25) and from leadership-turmoil reports I could not verify; P/E 18.8 with 83% growth looks cheap, but its latest filed results are from July and its 121% volatility is too high.

Too early to tell: P/E 14.2 with 22% growth looks cheap, but I found no company-specific cause for the 15% monthly fall, it trades with the AI-capex selloff with only a 0.6% free-cash-flow yield as capex rises, and it is 19% under its 200-day average.
Cheap (P/E 17.7, 8% free-cash-flow yield) and rising while the AI complex falls, but revenue growth is only 6.5%, and a 15th name in a sector I deliberately underweight is not a clear enough gain.

updates.lesson: Base exits on whether the earnings driver is breaking, not on price lines alone: Valero, sold as refining margins fell, kept falling (the sale helped by 4.5 points), while Fortinet, sold on a price rule after its drop, then beat the ETF by 3.9 points.

updates.alert: I'm selling Fortinet because my exit condition was met: it closed 5.6% below its 200-day average and is down 27% since purchase, 17 points behind the S&P 500 ETF. I'm buying Target. It reported a clear Q3 beat on November 18: sales +7.1%, comparable sales +5.6%, and it raised full-year guidance (about $0.50 of EPS came from one-off tariff refunds). It also rose 3% in a week when the index fell 7.7%, and it fills my zero consumer-staples weight. I'm also buying a smaller position in Omnicom. Organic growth accelerated to 7.2% in Q3 as the Interpublic integration nears completion, the free-cash-flow yield is 12%, the share is only 4% under its high, and it gives the portfolio its first communication-services exposure. I'm keeping Keysight: its November 19 results were a record (revenue +41%, orders +53%, ahead of guidance), so the business side of my exit condition is not met. I am tightening its exit rule because the share is 19% under its 200-day average. The main risks I'm watching are a further broad selloff, CrowdStrike and NetApp both reporting on December 1, and Morgan Stanley sitting just at its exit line.
updates.market_view: The S&P 500 ETF fell 7.7% this week and 9.1% over the month. Only 47% of members are still above their 200-day average, down from 57% three days ago, so the correction is spreading beyond tech. Tech is still the epicenter (sector median -15.5% over a month, with chips and hardware worst hit), and energy also fell 10% over the month. Staples, utilities and health care are the only sectors holding up, and companies with strong results (Target, Keysight) are reporting into a market that is selling almost everything.
updates.self_review: Since November 18 the portfolio trailed the ETF by 0.3 points. The Humana and Valero sales helped by 5.3 and 1.9 points, and Hasbro is 1.1 points ahead of the ETF. But keeping Fortinet, Keysight and NetApp through the tech slide hurt, and Fortinet now meets its exit condition, which I am acting on rather than loosening. Passing on MU (-13.5% since) was right; passing on TGT and OXY cost about 5 points each, so this time I am buying Target now that its results are confirmed.

new.thesis: Q3 (reported November 18) beat estimates: sales +7.1%, comparable sales +5.6%, traffic +5%, and full-year guidance raised. The share is 2% under its high and rose in a week when the index fell 7.7%, and it fills my zero staples weight at a P/E of 17.

Organic growth accelerated to 7.2% in Q3 as the Interpublic merger integration nears completion, with $900 million in targeted synergies. It has a 12% free-cash-flow yield, net cash, trades 4% under its high, and gives the portfolio its first communication-services exposure.

I'm deliberately skipping the most extreme momentum names, Moderna (+732% in 12 months), Lumentum and Bloom Energy, because their daily price swings are too wild to size sensibly. The main risks I'm watching: refining margins could fall back, the AI and tech selling could spread to my software names, and a broader pullback could hit Morgan Stanley through weaker capital-markets activity. These are judgments from the brief's price data only; I didn't run any news searches this week.

Test-and-measurement company with improving orders across AI, wireless and defense customers, and +104% 12-1 month momentum.
Leader in gene sequencing whose results are recovering. The stock is +36% over 3 months and 54% above its 200-day average.

Wealth-management franchise whose stock is 21% off its high. I'm making it a small position to add financials at a lower price.
